\chapter{Complexity — Games}
%%% generated by the blueprint pipeline from TCSlib.Complexity.ClassPSPACE.Games
\section{Overview}

Declarations of the Lean module \texttt{TCSlib.Complexity.ClassPSPACE.Games}.

\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Alternating-strategy play sequence]
\lean{Complexity.Game.playOut}
\label{Complexity.Game.playOut}
\leanok
Given two strategies $s_1,s_2 : \text{List}(\text{Bool})\to\text{Bool}$ and a natural
number $n$, the play sequence of length $n$ starts with the empty history and is formed
by repeatedly appending one bit: at an even-length history append the bit chosen by
$s_1$, and at an odd-length history append the bit chosen by $s_2$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[First player's winning strategy]
\lean{Complexity.Game.FirstWins}
\label{Complexity.Game.FirstWins}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.Game.playOut}
For a natural number $n$ and a Boolean-valued winning condition $W$ on finite Boolean
histories, the first player wins in $n$ steps if there is a strategy $s_1$ such that,
for every strategy $s_2$ of the second player, $W$ evaluates to true on the play of
length $n$ generated by these strategies.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Second player's winning strategy]
\lean{Complexity.Game.SecondWins}
\label{Complexity.Game.SecondWins}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.Game.playOut}
For a natural number $n$ and a Boolean-valued winning condition $W$ on finite Boolean
histories, the second player wins in $n$ steps if there is a strategy $s_2$ such that,
for every strategy $s_1$ of the first player, $W$ evaluates to false on the play of
length $n$ generated by these strategies.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Recursive value of a game position]
\lean{Complexity.Game.positionValue}
\label{Complexity.Game.positionValue}
\leanok
Given a Boolean-valued winning condition $W$ on finite Boolean histories, define the
value at a position $h$ with zero remaining steps to be $W(h)$. With $r+1$ steps
remaining, take the logical disjunction of the values at the two one-bit extensions of
$h$ when $h$ has even length, and their logical conjunction when $h$ has odd length.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[One move in alternating play]
\lean{Complexity.Game.ply}
\label{Complexity.Game.ply}
\leanok
Given strategies $s_1,s_2 : \text{List}(\text{Bool})\to\text{Bool}$ and a finite Boolean
history $h$, one move extends $h$ by the bit chosen by $s_1$ when $h$ has even length
and by $s_2$ when $h$ has odd length.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Successor play update]
\lean{Complexity.Game.playOut_succ_ply}
\label{Complexity.Game.playOut_succ_ply}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.Game.playOut, Complexity.Game.ply}
\difficulty{1}
For any two strategies assigning a Boolean move to each finite Boolean history and any
natural number $r$, the history after $r+1$ moves is obtained by applying one
single-move update to the history after $r$ moves, using the first player's strategy at
even-length histories and the second player's strategy at odd-length histories.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Play as repeated single moves]
\lean{Complexity.Game.playOut_eq_iterate}
\label{Complexity.Game.playOut_eq_iterate}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.Game.playOut, Complexity.Game.playOut_succ_ply, Complexity.Game.ply}
\difficulty{4}
For any two strategies assigning a Boolean move to each finite Boolean history and any
natural number $r$, the history after $r$ moves is the result of applying the
single-move update $r$ times to the empty history.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[First player's greedy choice]
\lean{Complexity.Game.firstGreedy}
\label{Complexity.Game.firstGreedy}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.Game.positionValue}
Given a natural number $n$, a Boolean-valued winning condition $W$ on finite Boolean
histories, and a history $h$, the first player's greedy choice is the value of the
recursive position evaluation at the history obtained by appending true to $h$, with
$\max(n-(|h|+1),0)$ steps remaining.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Second player's greedy choice]
\lean{Complexity.Game.secondGreedy}
\label{Complexity.Game.secondGreedy}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.Game.firstGreedy}
Given a natural number $n$, a Boolean-valued winning condition $W$ on finite Boolean
histories, and a history $h$, the second player's greedy choice is the Boolean negation
of the first player's greedy choice at $h$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Position value determines the winner]
\lean{Complexity.Game.winner_of_value}
\label{Complexity.Game.winner_of_value}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.Game.firstGreedy, Complexity.Game.ply, Complexity.Game.positionValue, Complexity.Game.secondGreedy}
\difficulty{6}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $W$ be a Boolean-valued predicate on finite Boolean
histories, let $s_1,s_2$ be strategies for the first and second players, and let $b$ be
a Boolean value. Define the value of a position with $r$ moves remaining recursively: at
zero remaining moves it is $W$ of the current history; otherwise it is the disjunction
of the two successor values when the history has even length, and their conjunction when
it has odd length. The first player's greedy strategy chooses true exactly when the
successor obtained by appending true has value true, and the second player's greedy
strategy is its Boolean negation. If $b=\mathrm{true}$ implies $s_1$ is the first
player's greedy strategy, if $b=\mathrm{false}$ implies $s_2$ is the second player's
greedy strategy, if the current history $h$ and the remaining number of moves satisfy
$|h|+r=n$, and if the position value at $(r,h)$ equals $b$, then after $r$ moves from
$h$ under $s_1,s_2$, the outcome $W$ equals $b$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Determinacy of the Boolean game]
\lean{Complexity.Game.determined}
\label{Complexity.Game.determined}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.Game.FirstWins, Complexity.Game.SecondWins, Complexity.Game.firstGreedy, Complexity.Game.playOut_eq_iterate, Complexity.Game.positionValue, Complexity.Game.secondGreedy, Complexity.Game.winner_of_value}
\difficulty{4}
Consider a game of $n$ moves in which the players alternately append a Boolean value to
the history, with the first player moving when the history has even length, and let $W$
be a Boolean-valued predicate on histories. Either the first player has a strategy that
guarantees $W$ is true at the resulting history, or the second player has a strategy
that guarantees $W$ is false.
\end{theorem}
